newsitem.title: USA: Corn, wheat and oil prices fall.
newsitem.headline: Corn, wheat and oil prices fall.

text.p: Corn and wheat prices fell Tuesday as crop prospects brightened, and oil prices also dropped as recent worries about heating oil supplies faded.

Commodities were hit again by speculative selling as worries about supplies, inflation and rising interest rates remained subdued. The Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 futures ended 0.39 point lower at 236.13, just off the day's new 12-month low at 235.99.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn and wheat prices fell to life-of-contract lows as optimism about available grain supplies increased.
December delivery wheat closed 11 cents lower at $3.68-3/4 a bushel, down 42 percent from its $6.32-3/4 high on April 25.

Weekly reports from state agronomists on Monday rated the young winter wheat crop planted from Texas to Ohio in 75 percent good or excellent condition. A larger-than-expected 93 percent of the crop was seeded as of Sunday.
Talk that the European Union and Argentina were aggressively offering to export wheat also prompted sales.

"It feels like total liquidation in here," said Skip Searcy, wheat trading specialist for FIMAT Futures in Chicago. "The conditions were negative, Argentina is offering wheat at $124 (a ton) and the EU is trying to get rid of wheat."
Wheat at the Port of New Orleans for December shipment was quoted at $164 to $175 a metric ton on Tuesday, compared with $124 at dockside on Argentina's Plate River, traders said.
December corn closed 3-1/4 cents lower at $2.58-1/2 a bushel, down 34 percent from its July 12 contract high.

Iowa-based analytical firm Farmers Commodities Corp. raised its forecast for the 1996 U.S. corn crop to 9.33 billion bushels, above average trade guesses as well as the government's Oct. 11 estimate of 9.012 billion.
Corn prices are now at a 14-month low.
"People on the floor were looking for a 9.2 (billion), so (Farmers Commodities) was a little bearish," said Ron Kucha of O'Connor and Co.
November soybeans closed 4 cents per bushel higher at $6.70 after Farmers Commodities pegged the soybean crop at 2.37 billion bushels, below traders' expectations of a 2.4 billion bushel figure.
A report from exporters that China recently bought 44,000 metric tons of U.S. soyoil and may seek more U.S. soybeans and soymeal also sparked buying.
Oil prices ended lower at the New York Mercantile Exchange ahead of weekly oil inventory data expected to show further increases in crude and heating oil stockpiles.

Heating oil for December delivery ended down 0.53 cent to 65.42 cents a gallon, December crude oil fell 15 cents to $22.64 a barrel, and December unleaded gasoline fell 0.39 cent to 64.61 cents a gallon.
"Gasoline was strong, especially in the cash market, but people are expecting a bearish build in distillates," said Ed Kevelson, director of refined products at Paribas Futures Inc.

The American Petroleum Institute reported after the NYMEX close, however, that distillate stocks -- heating oil and diesel -- fell a surprising 429,000 barrels in the week ended on Nov. 1 to 117.46 million barrels.
Distillates had risen 3.6 million barrels a week earlier, helping relieve fears about historically low heating fuel stocks in the Northeast this winter.
The API also said crude oil stocks rose 9.30 million barrels in the week to 312.42 million barrels, and gasoline stocks rose 4.74 million barrels to 190.76 million.

Doctors for Russia's President Boris Yeltsin declared his heart bypass operation a success Tuesday, but traders said the news was neutral to oil prices as it was another sign the Russian government would not be disrupted.
Russia is one of the world's largest oil producers.
